pos: n. (the hinder part of the body; the seat)
etymology: From butt, the thick or blunt end, with the diminutive ending. The Authorized Version uses the plural four times, and never idly: three of the four are about deliberate public humiliation, and the translators declined to look away.
biblical_def: Hanun's outrage against David's ambassadors is recorded twice in the same words, because it started a war: “Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away” (2 Samuel 10:4; compare 1 Chronicles 19:4). The insult was calculated to strip men of the two visible marks of standing, the beard and the robe, and David's answer was to tell them to tarry at Jericho till their beards were grown. Isaiah is given the same image as a prophecy against the nations Judah was tempted to trust: “So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt” (Isaiah 20:4). The prophet himself walked naked and barefoot three years as the sign. Scripture's plainness here is deliberate: the shame of captivity is bodily, and a nation that leans on Egypt is being warned in terms it cannot romanticize.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines buttock as the rump, or the protuberant part of the body behind; and in ships, the breadth of a ship astern.
webster_full: BUTTOCK, n. The rump, or the protuberant part of the body behind.
BUTTOCK, n. The convexity of a ship behind, under the stern.
RUMP, n. The end of the backbone of an animal, with the parts adjacent.
NAKED, a. Not covered; bare; having no clothes on; open to view; manifest.
SHAME, n. A painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt, or of having done something which injures reputation.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 10:4
Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away.
1 Chronicles 19:4
Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away.
Isaiah 20:4
So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.
2 Samuel 10:5
When they told it unto David, he sent to meet them, because the men were greatly ashamed: and the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.
corruption_summary: Two errors meet on a word like this — a squeamish piety that would not have the Bible say it, and a coarse age that says it for amusement; Scripture uses it soberly, to name a real shame inflicted on real men.
corruption_paragraphs: The first temptation is to tidy the Authorized Version. A translation committee that would soften 2 Samuel 10:4 into something decorous has already decided that the Bible needs protecting from itself, and the cost is the loss of what actually happened: envoys under the protection of their king were half-shaved and exposed in a foreign court, and a war followed. Scripture is not coarse, but it is candid, and candour about bodily humiliation is exactly what makes David's tenderness intelligible — he did not summon the men to Jerusalem to report; he sent word to tarry at Jericho until their beards were grown, and then he avenged them.

The opposite error belongs to a culture that has made the body a joke and public exposure an entertainment. Isaiah 20 forbids both the giggle and the shrug. The uncovering there is a judgment, the stripping of a proud nation, and the prophet bore the sign in his own person for three years. The principle to recover is that the body carries dignity because it is made and will be raised, that its deliberate exposure by another is a genuine injury, and that a king's first duty to men shamed in his service is to shelter them until the shame is past.
roots_summary: Hebrew shethah (H8357), the seat or buttocks; galach (H1548), to shave; arowm (H6174), naked; kalam (H3637), to be put to shame.
roots_lines: Hebrew shethah (H8357) — the seat, the buttocks; the word in 2 Samuel 10:4 and Isaiah 20:4.
Hebrew galach (H1548) — to shave, to make bald; half the beard taken from each ambassador.
Hebrew arowm (H6174) — naked, bare; the state of the Egyptian captives in Isaiah's sign.
Hebrew kalam (H3637) — to wound, to insult, to be put to shame; the men greatly ashamed.
Hebrew zaqan (H2206) — the beard; the mark of standing Hanun destroyed.
usage: “Cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks” — a calculated insult.
“Even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt” — judgment made visible.
“Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown” — a king sheltering shamed men.

etymology: Latin pallidus, pale, wan. The Authorized Version uses the adjective twice, and they are the two poles of the word: a promise that Jacob's face shall not wax pale, and the colour of the horse whose rider is Death.
biblical_def: Paleness in Scripture is the colour of fear and of shame drained into the face. Isaiah announces the end of it for the covenant people: “Therefore thus saith the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale” (Isaiah 29:22). The ground of the promise is redemption already accomplished — who redeemed Abraham — and the effect is on the countenance, because shame is a thing that shows. Over against it stands the fourth seal: “And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him” (Revelation 6:8). The Greek is chloros, the greenish pallor of a corpse; John gives the rider a name, which none of the other three receive, and a power limited to the fourth part of the earth. Between these two verses the believer lives: Death rides pale, and the redeemed face does not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pale as white or whitish; wan; deficient in color; not ruddy or fresh of color.
webster_full: PALE, a. White or whitish; wan; deficient in color; not ruddy or fresh of color; as, a pale face.
PALE, a. Not bright; not shining; of a faint lustre; dim; as, the pale light of the moon.
WAN, a. Pale; having a sickly hue; languid of look.
WAX, v.i. To increase in size; to grow; to become; as, to wax pale; to wax old.
ASHAMED, a. Affected by shame; abashed or confused by guilt or a conviction of some criminal action.
scriptures: Isaiah 29:22
Therefore thus saith the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale.
Revelation 6:8

And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth.
Isaiah 29:23
But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands, in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel.
Revelation 6:7
And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth beast say, Come and see.
corruption_summary: Death is managed now as a medical event to be delayed and a subject to be avoided, where Revelation names the rider, gives him a limit, and sets him under the authority of the Lamb who opened the seal.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern arrangement is to keep death out of sight: it happens in institutions, it is spoken of in euphemism, and the aim of a great deal of effort is to postpone the conversation rather than prepare for the event. Revelation 6:8 does the opposite. It paints the horse the colour of a corpse, names the rider Death, tells the reader that Hell followed with him, and states plainly how much power was given to them. Nothing about the vision is comfortable and everything about it is bounded — the power is given, the portion is a fourth, and the seal was opened by the Lamb that was slain.

Isaiah 29:22 is the counterweight and belongs preached beside it. God promises that the face of his people shall not wax pale, and he grounds it not in their strength but in his own prior act: the LORD who redeemed Abraham. The saint is not promised he will never see the pale horse; he is promised that shame will not have the last word in his countenance, because the redemption that took hold of Abraham has taken hold of him. A man who knows both verses can look steadily at a thing this culture cannot bear to name.
roots_summary: Hebrew chavar (H2357), to grow pale; bosh (H954), to be ashamed; padah (H6299), to redeem; Greek chloros (G5515), pale green.
roots_lines: Hebrew chavar (H2357) — to blanch, to wax pale; what Jacob's face shall not do.
Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, confounded; the shame paleness displays.
Hebrew padah (H6299) — to ransom, to redeem; the LORD who redeemed Abraham.
Greek chloros (G5515) — pale green, the colour of a corpse; the horse of the fourth seal.
Greek thanatos (G2288) — death; the only rider of the four who is given a name.
usage: “Neither shall his face now wax pale” — grounded in a redemption already done.
“Behold a pale horse... his name that sat on him was Death” — named and bounded.
“Power was given unto them” — given, and therefore limited.

pos: v.i. & n. (to bring forth young; a stock or race)
etymology: Old English bredan, to cherish or keep warm, hence to hatch. The Authorized Version uses the family for the multiplying of creatures after the flood, for a celebrated stock of rams, and for the breeding of nettles in a ruined land.
biblical_def: The word's first appearance is a commission given as the ark opened: “Bring forth with thee every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth; that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth” (Genesis 8:17). Breeding here is not a blind biological fact but a charge: God renews the creation mandate to the beasts as well as to Noah. The noun names a stock in the song of Moses, where God's bounty to Israel is inventoried — “Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan” (Deuteronomy 32:14). And the participle names a curse: Zephaniah says Moab shall be “as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation” (Zephaniah 2:9). The same earth that breeds cattle abundantly breeds nettles where God has withdrawn; fruitfulness is a gift, not a property of the ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines breed as to procreate; to generate; to hatch; to produce; and as a noun, a race or progeny from the same stock.
webster_full: BREED, v.t. To procreate; to generate; to beget; to hatch, as fowls do their young.
BREED, v.i. To produce, as a fetus; to bear and nourish, as in pregnancy.
BREED, n. A race or progeny from the same parents or stock.
BREED, n. A cast; a kind; a race of men or other animals which have an alliance by nativity.
MULTIPLY, v.i. To increase in number; to extend; to grow or become more numerous by propagation.
scriptures: Genesis 8:17

Bring forth with thee every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth; that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth.
Deuteronomy 32:14
Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the fat of kidneys of wheat; and thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape.
Zephaniah 2:9

Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them.
Genesis 9:1
And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.
corruption_summary: Fruitfulness is now treated as a problem to be managed and multiplication as a threat to the planet, against a Bible in which breeding abundantly is a blessing commanded by God and barrenness of ground is the curse.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant environmental account reverses Genesis 8. There multiplication is the aim, spoken over the beasts and then over Noah, and the earth's filling is the goal of the rescue rather than a danger created by it. The modern instinct treats human and animal increase alike as pressure on a finite system, and the corrective is not to deny finitude — Scripture is unsentimental about famine, drought and limits — but to refuse the premise that fruitfulness is itself the injury. God commanded the ark's creatures to breed abundantly in a world he had just emptied, and he called it good.

Zephaniah supplies the other half and keeps this from becoming naive. Ground can breed the wrong things. Moab and Ammon are sentenced to become the breeding of nettles and saltpits and a perpetual desolation, which is what a land does when God withdraws. Fruitfulness is therefore never a mechanism to be assumed but a mercy to be sought, and the recovery is stewardship under blessing: to keep and dress the earth as men who expect God to give the increase, and who know that the same soil grows nettles at his word.
roots_summary: Hebrew sharats (H8317), to swarm or breed abundantly; parah (H6509), to be fruitful; rabah (H7235), to multiply; memshaq (H4476), a possession or breeding-place.
roots_lines: Hebrew sharats (H8317) — to swarm, to breed abundantly; the charge to the creatures in Genesis 8:17.
Hebrew parah (H6509) — to bear fruit, be fruitful; the first half of the creation mandate.
Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to become many, to multiply; the second half, renewed after the flood.
Hebrew ben (H1121) — son; behind rams of the breed, literally sons, of Bashan.
Hebrew charul (H2738) — the nettle; what a cursed ground breeds instead.
usage: “That they may breed abundantly in the earth” — a commission, not a danger.
“Rams of the breed of Bashan” — God's bounty inventoried.
“Even the breeding of nettles” — what ground yields under judgment.

pos: n. (a companion; one of a pair)
etymology: Low German mate, a messmate, one who eats at the same table. The Authorized Version uses it twice, both in Isaiah 34, and the doctrine hanging on those two verses is larger than the word suggests.
biblical_def: Isaiah is describing Edom after judgment, a land given over to wild creatures: “There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate” (Isaiah 34:15). Then comes the astonishing verse that makes the bird-list a test of Scripture: “Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall want her mate: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them” (Isaiah 34:16). The prophet sends the reader to the written book and stakes God's veracity on the pairing of carrion birds in a desolated country. Two claims are made at once: that the smallest detail of prophecy will come to pass exactly, down to whether a vulture finds her mate; and that the gathering of these creatures is the work of God's own mouth and Spirit. The providence that pairs birds in a ruin is the providence that keeps the whole word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mate as a companion; an associate; one who customarily associates with another; also, a husband or wife.
webster_full: MATE, n. A companion; an associate; one who customarily associates with another.
MATE, n. A husband or wife; also, the male or female of animals which associate for propagation.
MATE, n. In ships, an officer who, in case of the master's death, takes his place.
COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Isaiah 34:15
There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate.
Isaiah 34:16
Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall want her mate: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them.
Matthew 10:29
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
Isaiah 34:17
And he hath cast the lot for them, and his hand hath divided it unto them by line: they shall possess it for ever, from generation to generation shall they dwell therein.
corruption_summary: Providence is commonly conceded in the large and denied in the small, as though God governs history but not the pairing of birds; Isaiah 34:16 makes the smallest detail the proof of the book.
corruption_paragraphs: It is a common half-faith to allow God the great movements and leave the small ones to chance. Isaiah 34:16 will not permit the division. The prophet has just listed the creatures that will inhabit a ruined Edom, and he tells the reader to go to the book of the LORD and read, because none shall want her mate. The veracity of Scripture is staked on the pairing of vultures. If prophecy is that exact in a detail no one could check for centuries, then the God who spoke it governs at that resolution everywhere, and our Lord teaches the same when he says a sparrow does not fall to the ground without our Father.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the pairing of God's word and God's Spirit in the verse: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them. What God says, God's Spirit effects. That is the ground of confidence in reading Scripture at all — the same breath that commanded is at work to accomplish — and the direct application is Isaiah's own: seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read.
roots_summary: Hebrew reuwth (H7468), a companion or mate (feminine); cepher (H5612), a book or scroll; peh (H6310), mouth; ruwach (H7307), spirit or breath.
roots_lines: Hebrew reuwth (H7468) — a female companion, a mate; none shall want her mate.
Hebrew cepher (H5612) — a writing, a book; the book of the LORD the prophet sends us to.
Hebrew peh (H6310) — the mouth; my mouth it hath commanded.
Hebrew ruwach (H7307) — wind, breath, Spirit; his spirit it hath gathered them.
Hebrew qabats (H6908) — to gather, to collect; the Spirit's work upon the creatures.
usage: “Every one with her mate” — providence at the smallest scale.
“Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read” — a command to check him.
“My mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them”.

pos: n. (a raft of timber borne on the water)
etymology: Old English flota, a ship or fleet, from fleotan, to float. In the Authorized Version the word is a noun and a technical one: the rafts of Lebanon cedar floated down the coast for the building of the temple.
biblical_def: Both occurrences describe the same operation, the shipping of Lebanon timber for Solomon's temple. Hiram proposes the method: “My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon unto the sea: and I will convey them by sea in floats unto the place that thou shalt appoint me, and will cause them to be discharged there, and thou shalt receive them” (1 Kings 5:9). The chronicler records the agreement kept: “And we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as thou shalt need: and we will bring it to thee in floats by sea to Joppa; and thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem” (2 Chronicles 2:16). A float is a raft — logs bound together and borne by the water that would have to be crossed anyway, moved by a current rather than by men. The detail is worth noticing because Scripture records it: the house of God was built with cedar that a Gentile king cut, a sea carried, and Israel hauled up from the coast. Ordinary logistics, faithfully done, is part of the building of a temple.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a float as a body so light as to swim on water; a quantity of timber fastened together and floated down a stream; a raft.
webster_full: FLOAT, n. A body so light as to swim on the surface of water; a raft.
FLOAT, n. A quantity of timber fastened together and floated down a stream or over a lake.
FLOAT, v.i. To be borne or buoyed on water; to swim; to be supported on the surface of a fluid.
RAFT, n. An assemblage of boards, planks or pieces of timber fastened together and floated down a stream.
CEDAR, n. The name of several species of coniferous trees, of which the cedar of Lebanon is the most celebrated.
scriptures: 1 Kings 5:9

My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon unto the sea: and I will convey them by sea in floats unto the place that thou shalt appoint me, and will cause them to be discharged there, and thou shalt receive them: and thou shalt accomplish my desire, in giving food for my household.
2 Chronicles 2:16
And we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as thou shalt need: and we will bring it to thee in floats by sea to Joppa; and thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem. as
1 Kings 5:6

Now therefore command thou that they hew me cedar trees out of Lebanon; and my servants shall be with thy servants: and unto thee will I give hire for thy servants according to all that thou shalt appoint: for thou knowest that there is not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians.
1 Kings 6:9
So he built the house, and finished it; and covered the house with beams and boards of cedar.
corruption_summary: The unglamorous labour behind sacred work is habitually left out of the story, where Scripture keeps the shipping contract in the record beside the glory that filled the house.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is one every church knows: to tell the story of God's work with the logistics edited out. Scripture refuses. The Holy Ghost preserved the terms of a timber contract, the route of the rafts, the port of Joppa and the haul up to Jerusalem, and put them in the same book as the cloud that filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister. The men who bound logs into floats were building the temple as truly as the men who overlaid it with gold.

The second recovery is that God used a pagan king's navy and a pagan king's foresters to build his house, and Hiram was glad to do it. Common grace furnishes real skill, and the church is not diminished by employing it honestly and paying for it — Solomon sent wheat and oil year by year. What Scripture never allows is borrowing the world's methods for the worship itself; the cedar came by sea from Tyre, but the pattern of the house came from God, and the distinction between the two is the whole of the difference.
roots_summary: Hebrew dobrah (H1702), a raft or float; erez (H730), cedar; yam (H3220), the sea; Yapho (H3305), Joppa.
roots_lines: Hebrew dobrah (H1702) — a raft, a float of timber; the word in 1 Kings 5:9 and 2 Chronicles 2:16.
Hebrew erez (H730) — the cedar; the timber of Lebanon Solomon bought.
Hebrew yam (H3220) — the sea; the highway the floats travelled.
Hebrew Yapho (H3305) — Joppa, beautiful; the port where the floats were discharged.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — the house; what all this labour was for.
usage: “I will convey them by sea in floats” — a current doing the hauling.
“In floats by sea to Joppa” — the contract kept, and recorded.
“Thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem” — the last mile was Israel's.

pos: v.i. (to open the mouth wide; to stare with open mouth)
etymology: Old Norse gapa, to open the mouth. In the Authorized Version the word belongs to the language of suffering: it is what enemies do with their mouths around a righteous man, and it supplies one of the most exact pictures in the psalm of the cross.
biblical_def: Job is the first to be so surrounded: “They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me” (Job 16:10). The same three motions — the open mouth, the blow, the gathering — recur in the twenty-second Psalm, where David's words outrun his own experience: “They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion” (Psalm 22:13). The psalm that begins with My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me describes gaping mouths, pierced hands and feet, and garments parted by lot, and the gospels record the crowd about the cross wagging their heads and railing. Job also uses the word wistfully, of the hireling who gapeth after the shadow and the reward of his work (Job 7:2), a man whose whole day is an open-mouthed longing for evening. To gape is to be wholly given to an appetite, whether of malice or of weariness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gape as to open the mouth wide, from sleepiness, dulness, wonder, or desire; and to stare with open mouth.
webster_full: GAPE, v.i. To open the mouth wide, from sleepiness, drowsiness or dulness; to yawn.
GAPE, v.i. To open the mouth for food, as young birds; to crave; to desire earnestly.
GAPE, v.i. To stare with open mouth, as in wonder or expectation.
RAVENING, ppr. Preying with rapacity; voracious; as, a ravening wolf.
REPROACH, v.t. To censure in terms of opprobrium or contempt; to upbraid.
scriptures: They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me.
Psalm 22:13
They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion.
Job 7:2
As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work:
Psalm 22:1
To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
corruption_summary: Psalm 22 is widely read as nothing more than David's bad day, its detail explained away as poetic convention, when the psalm supplies particulars that fit one crucifixion a thousand years later.
corruption_paragraphs: A long tradition of criticism reads Psalm 22 as an individual lament and treats the gaping mouths, the bones out of joint, the pierced hands and feet and the parted garments as stock imagery of distress. The church has never read it so, and neither did our Lord, who took its first line onto the cross and thereby claimed the whole psalm. The gospel writers then record the details as fulfilment rather than as coincidence: the soldiers casting lots, the passers-by reviling, the mouths open around a dying man. The psalm is Messianic because Christ made it his, and its precision is evidence rather than embroidery.

The pastoral use of the word is the second thing. Job 16:10 puts into three clauses what it feels like to be surrounded by open mouths, and the Bible does not tell a sufferer that the mockery is imaginary or that he should rise above it. It gives him a psalm in which the same thing happened to a better man, and which ends not in vindication of the sufferer's own strength but in a congregation praising God to the ends of the earth. The hireling of Job 7:2, gaping after the shadow, is likewise not scolded for wanting the day to end; he is described with sympathy, by a man who could not sleep.
roots_summary: Hebrew paar (H6473), to open wide the mouth; shaaph (H7602), to gasp or pant after; taraph (H2963), to tear as prey; ariy (H738), a lion.
roots_lines: Hebrew paar (H6473) — to open the mouth wide, to gape; Job 16:10 and Psalm 22:13.
Hebrew shaaph (H7602) — to gasp, to pant or long after; the hireling gapeth after the shadow.
Hebrew taraph (H2963) — to tear, to ravin; the ravening lion of Psalm 22:13.
Hebrew ariy (H738) — a lion; the figure for the enemies around the cross.
Hebrew azab (H5800) — to forsake; the verb of Psalm 22:1, which our Lord took as his own.
usage: “They have gaped upon me with their mouth” — Job surrounded.
“As a ravening and a roaring lion” — the psalm of the cross.
“As an hireling looketh for the reward of his work” — gaping after evening.

pos: v.t. (to dress food in a pan with oil)
etymology: Latin frigere, to roast or fry, through Old French frire. The Authorized Version uses the participle twice, both times of an offering, and both times the pan is one of several appointed ways a meat offering might be prepared.
biblical_def: The law of the peace offering appoints several forms of the accompanying bread: “If he offer it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving unleavened cakes mingled with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and cakes mingled with oil, of fine flour, fried” (Leviticus 7:12). Baked in the oven, baked in a pan, fried in the fryingpan — Leviticus provides for each, and each is holy. David's ordering of the Levites keeps the same distinctions centuries later: certain sons of Kohath were appointed “both for the shewbread, and for the fine flour for meat offering, and for the unleavened cakes, and for that which is baked in the pan, and for that which is fried, and for all manner of measure and size” (1 Chronicles 23:29). The permanence of the detail is the lesson. God appointed men whose lifelong charge was the frying pan of the sanctuary and the measuring of flour, and Scripture names the office without a hint of apology.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fry as to dress with fat or butter in a pan over a fire; to cook by the action of heat in a pan.
webster_full: FRY, v.t. To dress with fat, butter or oil, in a pan over a fire; to cook in a frying pan.
FRY, v.i. To be heated and agitated; to boil; to simmer.
FRYING-PAN, n. A pan with a long handle, used for frying meat and vegetables.
MEAT-OFFERING, n. In Scripture, an offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense, distinct from the animal sacrifices.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
scriptures: Leviticus 7:12

If he offer it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving unleavened cakes mingled with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and cakes mingled with oil, of fine flour, fried.
1 Chronicles 23:29

Both for the shewbread, and for the fine flour for meat offering, and for the unleavened cakes, and for that which is baked in the pan, and for that which is fried, and for all manner of measure and size;
Leviticus 2:5
And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in a pan, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mingled with oil. in a
Leviticus 2:7
And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in the fryingpan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.
corruption_summary: Ordinary domestic labour is treated as spiritually neutral at best, where Leviticus makes the pan, the oil and the fine flour matters of divine appointment and sets Levites over them for life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misjudgment is a persistent one in the church: a hierarchy of callings in which preaching and prayer are spiritual and cooking, measuring and cleaning are merely practical, tolerated for the sake of the real work. Leviticus 2 and 7 legislate the frying pan. 1 Chronicles 23:29 records that the house of God had men appointed over that which is fried and over all manner of measure and size, and their names are in the book. God does not have a secular staff.

The second point is the freedom inside the appointment. The meat offering might be baken in the oven, baken in a pan, or fried — three lawful forms, each with its own instructions, none of them superior. God prescribes what he prescribes and leaves genuine latitude where he leaves it, and the worshipper's liberty lies exactly there. The principle to recover is a high view of appointed ordinary work: a woman with a pan and a measure, doing what God assigned in the manner he allowed, is engaged in the service of the sanctuary.
roots_summary: Hebrew machabath (H4227), a flat plate or pan; marchesheth (H4802), a fryingpan; soleth (H5560), fine flour; minchah (H4503), a meat offering.
roots_lines: Hebrew machabath (H4227) — a flat plate or baking pan; one lawful form of the meat offering.
Hebrew marchesheth (H4802) — a stewing or frying pan; behind that which is fried.
Hebrew soleth (H5560) — fine flour; the substance measured by appointed Levites.
Hebrew minchah (H4503) — a gift, a meat offering; the bloodless offering these pans served.
Hebrew towdah (H8426) — thanksgiving, a confession of praise; the sacrifice of Leviticus 7:12.
usage: “Cakes mingled with oil, of fine flour, fried” — one appointed form of three.
“For that which is fried” — a lifelong Levitical charge.
“For all manner of measure and size” — exactness as service.

pos: v.i. & v.t. (to draw in air through the nose; to sniff at contemptuously)
etymology: Dutch snuffen, to snuff or sniff. The Authorized Version uses it of wild asses drawing in the wind in a drought, and — devastatingly — of priests sniffing in contempt at the altar of the LORD.
biblical_def: Jeremiah twice paints the wild ass in the high places: she is “a wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away?” (Jeremiah 2:24), a figure for Judah's untameable appetite after other gods; and in the drought, “the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass” (Jeremiah 14:6). The picture is of a creature drawing in air because there is nothing else to take in. Malachi turns the same verb on the priesthood, and it is among the sharpest sentences in the prophets: “Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering” (Malachi 1:13). The men whose office was the altar had come to sniff at it as at a bad smell, and the blemished animals in their hands were the proof.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines snuff as to draw in with the breath through the nose; and figuratively, to snuff at, to express contempt by the nose.
webster_full: SNUFF, v.t. To draw in with the breath through the nose; to inhale.
SNUFF, v.i. To snort; to draw air with violence up the nose; and figuratively, to express contempt.
SNUFF, n. The burning part of a candle wick, or that which has been charred by the flame.
WEARINESS, n. The state of being weary or tired; lassitude; that lassitude which is induced by exertion.
CONTEMPT, n. The act of despising; the act of viewing or considering and treating as mean, vile and worthless.
scriptures: Jeremiah 2:24

A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away? all they that seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her.
Jeremiah 14:6
And the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass.
Malachi 1:13

Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the LORD.
Malachi 1:14

But cursed be the deceiver, which hath in his flock a male, and voweth, and sacrificeth unto the Lord a corrupt thing: for I am a great King, saith the LORD of hosts, and my name is dreadful among the heathen.
corruption_summary: Boredom with worship is now excused as a matter of style and preference, when Malachi records God's own verdict on men who called his service a weariness and snuffed at it while still performing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest modern account of a wandering heart in worship is that the form is at fault — the music, the length, the manner — and the remedy is presentation. Malachi 1 treats the same complaint as sin and names it exactly: what a weariness is it, and ye have snuffed at it. The offering was still being brought. Nobody had left; the sacrifices continued; the priests were at the altar. What God saw was the nose wrinkled at his own table, and what he pointed to as evidence was not their liturgy but their livestock: the torn, the lame and the sick, because a man who despises the worship gives God what costs him least.

Jeremiah's wild ass supplies the other half of the diagnosis and it is bleaker. A creature in a drought stands in the high place and snuffs up the wind because there is no grass; a creature in her occasion snuffs the wind at her pleasure and no one can turn her away. Appetite untamed and appetite unfed look almost identical from outside. The recovery is not a better atmosphere but repentance and a costly offering — and the assurance that the LORD of hosts, whose name is dreadful among the heathen, is worth a man's best animal and his undivided attention.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaaph (H7602), to gasp or snuff up; naphach (H5301), to blow or puff at; telaah (H8513), weariness; mashchath (H4893), a corrupt or blemished thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaaph (H7602) — to gasp, to snuff up the wind; the wild ass of Jeremiah 2:24 and 14:6.
Hebrew naphach (H5301) — to blow, to puff at in contempt; ye have snuffed at it.
Hebrew telaah (H8513) — weariness, hardship; what the priests called God's service.
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to seize; the torn animals they brought instead.
Hebrew mashchath (H4893) — a blemish, a corrupt thing; the cursed deceiver's offering.

“They snuffed up the wind like dragons” — because there was no grass.
“Ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts” — contempt at the altar.

pos: v.t. & v.i. (to rouse from sleep; to excite to action)
etymology: Old English wacnian, to become awake. The Authorized Version keeps the older form beside awake and wake, and uses it for three very different rousings: a servant's ear, the heathen summoned to judgment, and a prophet shaken out of sleep.
biblical_def: The most precious use is in the third Servant Song, where the Servant's learning is a daily waking: “The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned” (Isaiah 50:4). The tongue that can speak to the weary is given to an ear that is wakened every morning; hearing precedes speaking, and both are God's work, repeated daily. Joel uses the word for a summons to judgment: “Let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there will I sit to judge all the heathen round about” (Joel 3:12). And Zechariah is himself the object of it: “And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep” (Zechariah 4:1) — the vision of the golden candlestick, and the word not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, are given to a man who had to be shaken awake to receive them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines waken as to be roused from sleep; and transitively, to rouse from sleep, and to excite to action or motion.
webster_full: WAKEN, v.i. To wake; to cease to sleep; to be awakened.
WAKEN, v.t. To excite or rouse from sleep.
WAKEN, v.t. To excite to action or motion; to rouse from a state of inaction.
AWAKE, v.t. To rouse from sleep; to excite from a state resembling sleep, as from death or stupidity.
WEARY, a. Having the strength much exhausted by toil or violent exertion; tired; fatigued.
scriptures: Isaiah 50:4

The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary: he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the learned.
Joel 3:12
Let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there will I sit to judge all the heathen round about.
Zechariah 4:1
And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep,
Zechariah 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The vocabulary of being awakened has been captured for political enlightenment, where Scripture uses waking for God's daily opening of an ear to his word and for the summons of the nations to judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The language of awakening now does duty for a political conversion: to be awake is to have seen through the structures of society, and the waking is self-administered or administered by a movement. Isaiah 50:4 describes a different operation altogether. He wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear — God does it, he does it daily, and the organ he wakes is the ear. What follows is not denunciation but the tongue of the learned, and the use to which that tongue is put is to speak a word in season to him that is weary. A waking that produces contempt for the weary has not come from this passage.

Joel and Zechariah fill out the picture. There is a waking that is a summons to the bar: let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, and it is God who sits to judge. And there is the waking of a prophet who was asleep and had to be shaken, and who then received the word that governs all genuine reformation — not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. Every real awakening in Scripture is God rousing men to hear him, and it issues in comfort for the weary and reverence before the Judge.

Hebrew limmuwd (H3928) — instructed, a disciple; the tongue and the ear of the learned.

“Let the heathen be wakened” — a summons to the valley of judgment.
“As a man that is wakened out of his sleep” — a prophet shaken awake.

etymology: Of Northern origin, akin to Old Norse skopa, to run. The Authorized Version uses it only of creation and of Christ: mountains skipping like rams, Lebanon skipping like a calf, and the Beloved leaping upon the mountains.
biblical_def: Every occurrence is a picture of joy in something too large to be moved. In the psalm of the voice of the LORD, the cedars break and then the mountains dance: “He maketh them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn” (Psalm 29:6). The Exodus psalm asks the mountains to explain themselves: “The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs” (Psalm 114:4), and then, turning to address them directly, “Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs?” (Psalm 114:6). The answer the psalm gives is that the earth trembled at the presence of the Lord. Then the Song sets the same verb on the Bridegroom: “The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song of Solomon 2:8). What the mountains do before God, the Beloved does upon the mountains — nothing in the landscape slows him when he comes for his bride.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines skip as to leap; to bound; to spring; to pass over lightly; and also, to pass without notice.
webster_full: SKIP, v.i. To leap; to bound; to spring; as a goat or lamb.
SKIP, v.i. To pass over or omit anything in reading or writing.
SKIP, v.t. To pass over or by; to omit; to miss.
BOUND, v.i. To leap; to jump; to spring; to move forward by leaps.
EXULT, v.i. To rejoice in triumph; to rejoice exceedingly at success or victory.
scriptures: Psalm 29:6
He maketh them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn.
Psalm 114:4
The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs.
Psalm 114:6
Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs?
Song of Solomon 2:8
The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.
corruption_summary: Nature is treated either as a machine that cannot respond or as a divinity to be worshipped; Scripture makes the hills glad before their Maker without ever confusing them with him.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors crowd around a verse like Psalm 114:4. The first is a flattened naturalism in which the creation is mere mechanism, and the poetry of skipping mountains is a pretty way of saying nothing. The second is the sacralizing of nature itself, in which the earth is a mother and creation the object rather than the choir of worship. Scripture holds a third thing steadily: the hills really do rejoice, the trees of the field clap their hands, and every bit of it is directed at the presence of the Lord, who made them and is not one of them.

The Song supplies the reason such joy is not sentimental. The same verb that moves mountains describes the Beloved coming for his bride — leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills — and the barriers that would stop anyone else are what he travels on. The mountains skip because God is present; the Bridegroom skips because his bride is waiting. A creation that exults before its Maker and a Saviour who comes swiftly for his people are the same doctrine viewed from two sides, and the right response to both is the psalm's: tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew raqad (H7540), to skip about, to dance; ayil (H352), a ram; chuwl (H2342), to writhe or tremble; dalag (H1801), to leap.
roots_lines: Hebrew raqad (H7540) — to stamp, to spring about, to dance; the skipping of Psalm 114:4.
Hebrew ayil (H352) — a ram; the figure for the mountains at Sinai.
Hebrew dalag (H1801) — to leap, to spring; the Beloved leaping upon the mountains.
Hebrew chuwl (H2342) — to twist, to writhe, to tremble; the earth at the presence of the Lord.
Hebrew qowl (H6963) — a voice; the voice of the LORD that breaks cedars, and of the Beloved.
usage: “He maketh them also to skip like a calf” — Lebanon at the voice of the LORD.
“The mountains skipped like rams” — and the psalm asks them why.
“Leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” — the Bridegroom's speed.
